_comment: Storyboard for the Grade 4 Science unit lecture film, Lesson 5 Habitats and Survival. Rendered by tools/create-ehel-unit-lecture.js. See lecture-video/BRIEF.md. Every beat is one narration clip; art.at names the phrases a picture waits for, and the page refuses to load if a phrase is not in its beat's say. The chapters follow LESSON lecture in content/lesson-5.py in order (suited to the place; why it matters; surviving somewhere else; science near you; both sides), with one chapter added between the third and fourth for 4TWSp.01, which the lesson teaches in its ask step. The pictures are the lesson's own: the sort's four bins and their first four animals, the explore step's camel and polar bear features, the lookup step's fact card (food, water, temperature, shelter; the goldfish, the rainforest plant, the camels in Australia), the ask step's woodlice under a damp and a dry patch, and the context step's road, streetlights, recycling centre and park pond.
title: Habitats and Survival
subtitle: Grade 4 Science
objectives: Know that different animals are found in, and suited to, different habitats.
Know plants and animals can survive in environments other than their habitats.
Use secondary information sources to research an answer to a question.
Ask scientific questions that can be investigated.
Describe how science is used in their local area.
Discuss how the use of science and technology can have positive and negative environmental effects on their local area.

beats.say: A camel lives in the hot desert. A polar bear lives in the cold Arctic.
Each is suited to its home. Could it live anywhere else?
A habitat is where an animal lives in the wild. Here are four.
A camel in the desert, a polar bear in the Arctic. A monkey in the rainforest, a whale in the ocean.
Its features suit its habitat. A feature is a part of its body.
A camel has a hump of fat, and wide feet for the sand.
Long lashes keep sand out of its eyes. Every feature suits the desert.
A polar bear has thick fur over a layer of fat. So the Arctic cold does not reach it.
Put a polar bear in the desert, and its fur would cook it.
Put a fish in the desert, and its gills have no water to breathe.
The features that suit one place are wrong for another.
Can a living thing survive outside its habitat? Look it up on a fact card.
The card says yes: food, water, the right temperature and shelter.
A goldfish lives in a bowl: a person feeds it and keeps the water clean.
A rainforest plant lives on a windowsill, if a person waters it and keeps it warm.
Camels taken to Australia survived. Its hot, dry centre is like their home.
Give it what it needs, and it survives.
A scientific question is one you can investigate, by observing, counting or testing.
Are woodlice happy? You cannot go and check that.
Are more woodlice found in damp places than dry ones? You can count them.
Count under a damp patch and a dry patch, the same size, at the same time.
Only the dampness is different. That is a fair test.
Science and technology are all over your area. Technology is what people make and use.
Think of roads, streetlights, recycling centres and park ponds. Each changes habitats nearby.
A new road brings shops and jobs. But it cuts a habitat in two.
A pond dug in a park is a new habitat, for frogs and dragonflies.
Most technology helps some living things, and harms others.
Streetlights make streets safer at night. But moths fly round them until they drop.
Science lets you see both sides, and decide.
Its features suit its habitat, wrong for another place.
A fact card said it can survive, if given what it needs.
A good question is one you can go and check.
Technology near you helps some, harms others. Weigh up both sides.
